title: Async & Promises
description: Type asynchronous operations with Promise<T>, async/await, and parallel execution patterns.

challenges.title: What does async return?
challenges.whyMatters: Knowing that async functions always return a Promise — even when you write `return "hello"` — is the most important mental model for async TypeScript.
hints: async functions automatically wrap the return value in a Promise

challenges.title: First async function
challenges.description:
Write two async functions:

`delay(ms: number): Promise<void>` — resolves after `ms` milliseconds using `setTimeout`.

`greetAfterDelay(name: string, ms: number): Promise<string>` — waits for the delay, then returns `"Hello, name!"`.
challenges.whyMatters: Every async chain starts with a promise-wrapped primitive like setTimeout — understanding how to create and consume them is the foundation.
hints: Wrap the callback-based setTimeout in a Promise constructor — the resolve function should be called when the timer fires
Use await inside greetAfterDelay: await delay(ms)

challenges.title: Typed error handling
challenges.description:
Write `safeDivide(a: number, b: number): Promise<number>` that:
- Rejects with `new Error("Cannot divide by zero")` if b is 0
- Otherwise resolves with a / b

Then write `trySafeDivide(a: number, b: number): Promise<string>` that:
- Returns `"Result: X"` on success
- Returns `"Error: message"` on failure (caught)
challenges.whyMatters: try/catch with async/await is the standard error handling pattern — you must handle rejections explicitly or they become uncaught exceptions.
hints: Use throw inside an async function to reject: throw new Error(...)
Catch errors with try { ... } catch (err) { if (err instanceof Error) ... }

challenges.title: Chaining promises
challenges.description:
Write a pipeline of three async functions:

`fetchNumber(): Promise<number>` — resolves with 42.

`doubleAsync(n: number): Promise<number>` — resolves with n * 2.

`pipeline(): Promise<string>` — calls fetchNumber, passes result to doubleAsync, returns `"Result: 84"`.
challenges.whyMatters: Chaining async operations is the core pattern in any multi-step flow — fetch data, transform it, format it, return it.
hints: fetchNumber and doubleAsync each resolve with a single hard-coded value — pipeline chains them: await each result in order and pass it to the next call
In pipeline, await each async call in sequence — store the result and pass it as the argument to the next function

challenges.title: Promise.all — parallel
challenges.description:
Write three async functions that each resolve after a short delay:
- `fetchName(): Promise<string>` → resolves with `"Alice"`
- `fetchAge(): Promise<number>` → resolves with `30`
- `fetchRole(): Promise<string>` → resolves with `"admin"`

Then write `fetchAll(): Promise<string>` that runs all three in parallel and returns `"Alice, 30, admin"`.
challenges.whyMatters: Promise.all is critical for performance — running independent async operations in parallel instead of sequentially can cut total time by 2-3x.
hints: Pass all three function calls into Promise.all as an array — you can destructure the resolved tuple to get each typed value separately
Join the three resolved values with comma-space separators in a template literal

challenges.title: Promise.allSettled — tolerant parallel
challenges.description:
Write `checkAll(urls: string[]): Promise<{ url: string; ok: boolean }[]>` that:
- Calls `ping(url): Promise<boolean>` for each URL in parallel using `Promise.allSettled`
- Returns results for ALL urls — even if some ping calls reject, mark those as ok: false

Provide the mock: `ping(url)` resolves with `true` immediately.
challenges.whyMatters: Promise.allSettled is the right tool when you can't let one failure cancel everything — health checks, fan-out requests, batch operations.
hints: Map each URL to a ping call and pass the whole array to Promise.allSettled — every URL gets a result regardless of success or failure
Each settled result has a status field — check whether it is 'fulfilled' to decide whether to use its value or fall back to false

challenges.title: Sequential vs parallel
challenges.description:
Write `processSequential(items: number[]): Promise<number[]>` that processes items one by one — each item is doubled by an async `processItem(n: number): Promise<number>` function.

Then write `processParallel(items: number[]): Promise<number[]>` that processes all items at once using Promise.all.

Provide processItem: it resolves with n * 2.
challenges.whyMatters: Knowing when to use sequential vs parallel is a performance decision you'll make constantly — sequential for dependent operations, parallel for independent ones.
hints: Sequential: use a for...of loop with await inside, push to a results array
For the parallel version, map each item to a processItem call — collect all the promises and resolve them at once

challenges.title: AbortController
challenges.description:
Write `fetchWithTimeout(url: string, timeoutMs: number): Promise<string>` that:
- Creates an AbortController
- Sets a timeout that aborts the controller after `timeoutMs` ms
- Calls a mock `get(url, signal)` with the abort signal
- Clears the timeout if the fetch succeeds (use try/finally)
- If aborted, re-throws the error naturally

Provide the mock: `get(url, signal)` resolves with the url string immediately.
challenges.whyMatters: AbortController is the standard cancellation mechanism in modern JS/TS — fetch, streams, and many APIs accept an AbortSignal.
hints: const controller = new AbortController()
Set a timer that calls abort on the controller after the timeout duration — store the reference so you can cancel it in the finally block
Use try/finally to guarantee the timer is cancelled whether the fetch succeeds or throws — the finally block always runs

challenges.title: Bring it together
challenges.description:
Write a typed data pipeline with error handling:

`interface DataResult<T> { data: T | null; error: string | null; duration: number }`

`withTiming<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<DataResult<T>>` — runs fn, captures how long it took (Date.now()), returns a DataResult with either the data or the error message.

Then write `runPipeline(items: number[]): Promise<DataResult<number[]>>` that doubles all items in parallel (use Promise.all) wrapped in withTiming.
challenges.whyMatters: Combining parallel execution, timing, and typed error handling is the pattern behind every observability-aware service client you'll ever write.
hints: const start = Date.now()
In the try block, await fn() and build a result object with the data, a null error, and the elapsed time since start
In the catch block, return null data — narrow the caught error to extract a string message, and include the elapsed time
runPipeline: wrap a Promise.all over the doubled items inside withTiming — pass an arrow function returning the Promise.all so withTiming can time the whole parallel operation
